seed.relationship: two neighbors with a shared wall
seed.conflict: when old loyalties collide with new ones
seed.topicSeed: a lighthouse station in Manila; two neighbors with a shared wall when old loyalties collide with new ones

g.passage: Manila Bay's lighthouse station had two keepers' cottages joined by a single wall, and for eleven years I shared it with Wira. We knocked twice each evening to say the lamp was lit. When the bureau assigned Mateo to replace her, I resented him on principle, and for weeks I let his knocks go unanswered. Then one night the generator failed, and Mateo climbed the tower with me, holding the flashlight steady while I reset the breaker. Afterward he asked how Wira used to signal, and I found myself teaching him the double knock. Keeping that small ritual alive, I realized, honored her more than my silence ever had. Below us, the fishing boats rocked in a row, their lanterns swinging like loose buttons on a coat.
g.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To recount how the narrator and Mateo worked together to repair a generator that failed one night
To explain how the bureau organized the routines that keepers followed for lighting the lamp
To show how the narrator comes to see that welcoming a newcomer can preserve an old bond
To suggest that people must eventually let go of the past entirely in order to be happy
g.explanation: 앞부분에서 화자는 Wira와의 오랜 의리 때문에 새로 온 Mateo의 노크를 외면하지만, 뒷부분에서는 그에게 Wira의 두 번 노크를 가르치며 그 의식을 이어 가는 것이 오히려 Wira를 기리는 일임을 깨닫는다. 두 곳의 대비를 연결하면 새 이웃을 받아들이는 것이 옛 유대를 지키는 길이 될 수 있다는 C가 요지다. A는 발전기 수리 일화만 요약했고, B는 등대 소재를 쓰지만 서술 목적이 다르다. D는 과거를 완전히 버리라는 지나치게 일반적인 교훈으로, 지문은 오히려 과거를 이어 간다.

g.passage: “Leave the back panel; we only need to replace the shelf,” Okja said, handing over the chisel. In the quiet reading room of the Hokkaido library, Caoimhe pried loose the warped board and found an envelope wedged behind it, addressed in faded ink to someone named only as the Thursday reader. That morning the librarian had mentioned an elderly man who came every Thursday and always ran his hand along this very shelf before sitting down. Caoimhe studied the envelope, then cut a shallow groove into the new board, just deep enough to hold it. Okja raised an eyebrow but said nothing about the extra hour it cost. Outside, snow slid from the roof in a long, soft rush.
g.question: Based on the text, why does Caoimhe most likely cut a groove into the new board?
options: She worries that Okja will scold her for disturbing the back panel he told her to leave alone.
She hopes the extra hour of careful work will impress Okja with her skill as a carpenter.
She wants the envelope to stay where the man who visits on Thursdays might still find it.
She believes the library has a rule requiring any lost papers to be stored inside shelves.
g.explanation: 봉투가 'Thursday reader'에게 쓰여 있다는 점과, 사서가 말한 매주 목요일 이 선반을 손으로 쓸어 보는 노인이 있다는 점을 연결하면 Caoimhe가 편지를 원래 자리에 남겨 두려 한다는 동기가 드러난다. 따라서 C가 정답이다. A는 Okja에 대한 걱정이라는 다른 감정에서 나온 동기이고, B는 '추가 한 시간'이라는 결과를 동기로 착각한 것이다. D는 지문에 없는 도서관 규칙이라는 외부 원인을 끌어왔다.

g.passage: Rusted shears in hand, Annika knelt beside the tomato bed she and her brother Cyrus kept behind the community hall in Porto Alegre. That morning, hunting for twine in the shop's counter drawer, she had found a stack of overdue notices he had hidden beneath the receipt book. Now Cyrus arrived with two cups of coffee and a story about how well the week's sales had gone. Annika let him finish, then mentioned lightly that she had already sold her bicycle and would put the money toward the electricity bill. He stared at her, set down the cups, and quietly began tying up the vines she had missed. Across the garden, an old woman was scattering crushed eggshells around her lettuce.
g.question: Based on the text, which choice best describes the relationship between Annika and Cyrus?
options: They are siblings who each try to shield the other from the strain of the shop's troubles.
Annika resents Cyrus for hiding the shop's overdue notices and means to confront him.
Cyrus depends on Annika to make every decision about the shop and its unpaid bills.
They are rivals competing over the shop to prove which of them deserves to run it.

g.passage: Tar and wet hemp, that was the smell of every crossing. I was fourteen the summer Budi began riding our barge up the estuary from the Cornish coast, always with a sealed parcel on his knees and never with a fare in his hand. Father had told me only that Budi had once pulled him from the water at Falmouth, and that I, Abena, was not to ask for money. Each morning I spliced the frayed end of our mooring line, and each evening it had worn through again against the iron ring. Budi watched me work the strands together and once offered to buy us new rope. I said the old one would hold, and he did not argue. By September the splice was thicker than the rope itself, a knot of patches I could have tied blindfolded. On his last crossing he set his parcel down, took the line from me, and wove one strand in himself before stepping ashore without a word.
g.question: In the text, the repeatedly mended mooring line most likely represents
options: the ferryman's pride in the river skills he has passed down to his daughter.
the unspoken obligation that keeps the narrator's family and Budi bound together.
the growing danger of carrying passengers across the estuary in a worn barge.
the narrator's private wish to escape her father's trade on the river someday.
g.explanation: Budi는 아버지의 목숨을 구한 일 때문에 운임을 내지 않고, 아무도 그 빚을 말하지 않는다. 매일 끊어지고 다시 이어지는 밧줄, 새 밧줄을 사 주겠다는 제안을 거절하는 장면, 마지막에 Budi가 직접 한 가닥을 엮어 넣는 장면이 이어지며 밧줄은 양쪽을 묶는 말없는 의무를 상징하게 되므로 B가 정답이다. A는 기술 전수, C는 위험, D는 떠나고 싶은 마음을 말하지만 지문에 그런 단서가 없다.

g.passage: What do you say to a man who returns your present before he has even opened it? For three years I clerked for Bartolo in the courthouse above the harbor, and when he retired to take English lessons at a small language school in Valparaiso, I bought him a leather notebook for his vocabulary lists. On Tuesday he set it on my desk in the empty classroom, still in its tissue paper, and said he could not accept gifts from someone whose career he might yet be asked to recommend. His voice was the same one he had used from the bench, courteous and final. I held the package and felt I had been handed a verdict wrapped in tissue paper. Later, Camila, the teacher, asked me to help stack the chairs, and I did it slowly, listening to the gulls.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a verdict wrapped in tissue paper” most nearly suggests that the narrator
options: believes Bartolo has secretly decided to report her conduct to the court.
thinks the notebook was wrapped too carelessly to be offered as a gift.
experiences the return as a firm judgment delivered with gentle politeness.
suspects Bartolo is pretending to be stern to conceal his real gratitude.
g.explanation: Bartolo는 선물을 뜯지도 않고 돌려주며 원칙적인 이유를 대고, 그의 목소리는 법정에서처럼 '정중하지만 단호했다'. 이 두 단서를 연결하면 '판결'은 되돌릴 수 없는 단호한 결정을, '얇은 포장지'는 그것이 부드럽고 예의 바르게 전달되었음을 뜻하므로 C가 정답이다. A는 판결이라는 단어를 법적 고발로 지나치게 문자적으로 읽었고, B는 포장지를 문자 그대로 받아들였다. D는 지문에 근거가 없는 숨은 감사를 가정한다.

seed.relationship: a daughter and her absent father's friend

seed.topicSeed: a beekeeper's yard in Karachi; a daughter and her absent father's friend after a quiet act of generosity

g.passage: By the third week of the monsoon, Sunethra had stopped expecting her father's letters and started counting the hives instead. Seven boxes stood along the wall of the yard in Karachi; the eighth had gone silent in April, its colony lost to mites. Lanying, who had shared a shop with her father before he sailed, came by most evenings to drink tea and talk of nothing in particular. She never mentioned bees. Yet one damp morning Sunethra lifted the lid of the eighth box and found it thick with a new swarm, the frames already beaded with wax. When she asked, Lanying only shrugged and spoke about the price of sugar. Her kindness, Sunethra thought, moved through the yard like smoke through a hive, calming everything and leaving nothing behind. That afternoon the rain came again, drumming on the tin roof of the shed.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “like smoke through a hive” most nearly suggests that Lanying's help was
options: irritating to the bees and unsettling to the rest of the yard.
brief and fleeting, so that Sunethra soon forgot about it.
heavy and oppressive, making the yard hard to breathe in.
quietly soothing and difficult to trace back to its source.
g.explanation: Lanying은 벌 이야기를 한 번도 꺼내지 않았고, 새 벌 떼에 대해 묻자 어깨만 으쓱하고 설탕 값 이야기로 넘어간다. 양봉에서 연기는 벌을 진정시키지만 흔적을 남기지 않으므로, 두 단서를 연결하면 그녀의 도움이 조용히 위로가 되면서도 출처를 드러내지 않았다는 D가 정답이다. A는 연기를 벌을 자극하는 것으로, C는 숨 막히는 것으로 오해한 해석이다. B는 금방 잊혔다고 하지만 Sunethra는 그 친절을 곱씹고 있다.

seed.conflict: over how to mark an anniversary
seed.topicSeed: a tea plantation in Port of Spain; best friends after a move over how to mark an anniversary

g.passage:
What would Ivy want, Ronan wondered,
now that an ocean sat between them
and the date they had always kept came round again?
Above Port of Spain the tea rows climbed
like green stitches holding the slope together,
and he walked them at dawn, as the two of them once had,
pinching the youngest leaves the way she taught him.
Last year she had written that she kept no calendars now,
that each new street was busy erasing the old ones.
So he would send no card, no ribbon, nothing she must answer.
He dried one handful of leaves on the windowsill
and mailed them folded in plain brown paper,
a small country she could steep and drink alone.
The pickers' songs drifted up from the lower terraces,
thin and bright in the cooling air.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a small country she could steep and drink alone” most nearly suggests that the leaves are
options: a piece of their shared place that Ivy can savor privately, without having to reply.
a reminder of the home Ronan hopes Ivy will one day come back to and settle in.
a costly gift meant to show Ivy how well the plantation has prospered since then.
a sign of the distance that has turned Ronan and Ivy into strangers to each other.
g.explanation: Ronan은 Ivy가 이제 달력을 지키지 않는다는 편지를 떠올리고 '그녀가 답해야 할 것은 아무것도' 보내지 않기로 한다. 함께 걷던 차밭의 잎을 보내며 그것을 '혼자 우려 마실 작은 나라'라고 부르므로, 두 단서를 이으면 공유한 장소의 한 조각을 부담 없이 홀로 즐기게 한다는 A가 정답이다. B는 귀환에 대한 바람을, C는 값비싼 과시를 가정하지만 지문에 근거가 없다. D는 거리를 말하지만 시는 단절이 아닌 배려를 그린다.

g.passage: Bailing with a soup pot, I stood knee-deep in the cellar of the Galway town hall in the spring of 1987 while Aoife, our mayor, held the torch. Somewhere down here, in a crate marked with a boy's surname, was his late grandfather's accordion, and Aoife had sworn to the boy at the funeral that it would be kept safe. She had said so before the river rose, before anyone knew the drains would fail. Even I, Chiara, the town's only doctor, have made my share of reckless reassurances at bedsides, so I did not scold her. Her promise, I thought, had been a paper boat set on a calm puddle, and now the puddle was a flood. We found the crate on a high shelf, damp at one corner, and Aoife laughed so hard she nearly dropped the torch. Upstairs, the clerk was ringing every household on the low road.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a paper boat set on a calm puddle” most nearly suggests that Aoife's promise was

sincere but made before she could foresee the danger to come.
carefully planned to withstand any disaster the town might face.

g.passage: When we came back to Jeju Island in the autumn of 1898, my father, Taeyang, would not walk past the cemetery gate where his own father lay. He had left the island a young man and returned with a daughter who spoke English better than Korean, and I think he feared the dead would hear the difference. Each Sunday I, Gil, asked whether we might go in, and each Sunday he said the path was too muddy. Yet by midwinter he had begun stopping at the gate to straighten its leaning post, and once I saw him brush the moss from the nearest stone with his cuff. His refusal, I understood, had worn as thin as a winter sleeve. In March he asked me to teach him the English word for chrysanthemum, though he never said why. The gate creaked on its hinge as the wind came off the sea.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “worn as thin as a winter sleeve” most nearly suggests that Taeyang's
options: reasons for avoiding the cemetery had always been weak and insincere.
health had been steadily failing during the cold island winter.
resistance had gradually weakened until it barely held at all.
poverty had left him unable to afford proper graveside offerings.
g.explanation: 처음에 Taeyang은 매주 길이 질다며 묘지에 들어가기를 거부했지만, 한겨울쯤에는 문 기둥을 바로 세우고 소맷부리로 비석의 이끼를 닦는다. 오래 입어 닳은 겨울 소매처럼 그의 거부가 서서히 약해져 거의 남지 않았다는 뜻이므로 C가 정답이다. A는 '얇다'를 처음부터 약했다는 뜻으로 오독했고, 지문은 점진적 변화를 보여 준다. B는 겨울과 건강을, D는 낡은 옷과 가난을 문자적으로 연결한 오답이다.

g.passage: Wringing out a cloth in the basin, Savitri listened to the pickers singing below the veranda of the vineyard house outside Mumbai. Her patient, Sharda, had not slept for three nights, and tonight she was in a mood to accuse. Had Savitri not insisted on the fever cure, Sharda declared, she would have been fit to travel to the conservatory in Poona and sing for its masters; the letter had come and gone while she lay here. Savitri set her jaw and recited, in a clipped voice, every dose of physic she had measured out. Then Sharda's hand slid across the coverlet and closed on her wrist, and the old woman whispered that she had known for years her voice was gone, that it was easier to blame a nurse than a throat. Savitri sat down slowly on the edge of the bed. She told Sharda about the grape baskets stacked by the press, purple to the brim, and Sharda listened with her eyes closed, smiling. Down the hill, the singing stopped, and a lantern moved toward the sheds.
g.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: It moves from defensive tension to gentle sympathy once Sharda confesses why she blamed Savitri.
It moves from cheerful hope to bitter resentment after Sharda learns the conservatory rejected her.
It moves from calm routine to sudden alarm as Sharda's fever grows worse during the long night.
It moves from quiet sorrow to playful teasing as Savitri describes the grape harvest to Sharda.
g.explanation: 처음에 Sharda는 기회를 놓친 책임을 Savitri에게 돌리고, Savitri는 턱을 굳힌 채 딱딱한 목소리로 투약 기록을 읊어 방어적 긴장이 흐른다. 그러다 Sharda가 목소리는 이미 오래전에 사라졌고 목보다 간호사를 탓하는 게 쉬웠다고 고백하자, Savitri는 천천히 침대에 앉아 포도 이야기를 들려준다. 따라서 긴장에서 다정한 공감으로 바뀐다는 A가 정답이다. B는 거절 통보가 없고, C는 열이 악화되지 않으며, D는 장난스러운 분위기로 볼 근거가 없다.

g.passage: When Brigid swept into the dining hall of the boys' summer camp outside Glasgow, she meant to have it out with Esteban before the soup was served. Her brother had written home of a broken window and a week of extra lessons, and the tutor, it seemed, had told the camp master nothing at all about who had thrown the stone. Brigid laid the letter beside his plate and demanded to know what sort of guardian kept such things from a family. Esteban folded his napkin with great care. The stone, he said quietly, had been thrown at her brother, not by him, and the boys who threw it were the sons of the men who paid for the camp. Had he spoken, it was her brother who would have been sent home. Brigid sat down on the bench across from him, and for some time neither of them touched the bread. At the far end of the hall, a bell was rung for grace, and two hundred chairs scraped at once.
g.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: from playful teasing to open hostility as Brigid learns about the broken window

from anxious worry to cheerful relief as Brigid learns her brother is unharmed
from formal politeness to bitter despair as Esteban admits he has failed the boy

g.passage: Years later, the daughter would write that she had never hated anyone so thoroughly as the crowd at the Bologna ferry terminal on the morning her mother fainted against the ticket rail. Her mother had insisted on traveling alone, had refused the daughter's arm on the stairs, and then had crumpled in front of forty strangers, her hat rolling under a bench. The daughter remembered every stare and every whisper, and she recorded them in her diary with a cold, exact fury. But the essay turns on the next detail: Giacomo, the porter, retrieving the hat, brushing it with his sleeve, and handing it not to the daughter but to the mother, as though she were a lady who had merely dropped it. From that point the daughter's sentences loosen. She describes her mother pinning the hat back on with trembling dignity, and the two of them laughing, later, over the porter's grand bow. The ferry, she notes, left forty minutes late that day, its whistle echoing along the canal.
g.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: from cheerful nostalgia to sudden grief when the mother collapses at the terminal
from calm reporting to anxious urgency as the daughter rushes to find medical help
from bitter resentment to warm gratitude after Giacomo's courteous gesture

g.passage: “You always did eat too fast,” Leopoldina said, as Thiago bent over his bowl at the noodle stall behind the cemetery in Lisbon. It was the spring of 1924, and they had not spoken in eleven years. The funeral of their grandmother had brought them back to the same table, and the question of what to do with Leopoldina's aging father hung between them like steam. Thiago thought the old man should come to Porto; Leopoldina said he would wither away from the river. They argued in short, cool sentences, each correcting the other's memory of whose fault the long silence had been. Then the stall keeper set down a dish of fried dough without being asked, and Thiago recognized it as the treat their grandmother had bought them every Sunday as children. Leopoldina laughed despite herself and pushed the plate toward him. They began to talk of her father's fig tree, and of how he might be persuaded to visit both cities in turn. A tram rattled past, scattering pigeons from the cobbles.

from guarded argument to renewed warmth after a reminder of their shared childhood

seed.topicSeed: a school gymnasium in Kingston; a mother and a daughter planning a wedding about the last item in a house being emptied

g.passage: We had rented the school gymnasium in Kingston for the reception because it was cheap and because my mother had taught there for thirty years. That Saturday we walked its floor with a tape measure, arguing over where the long tables should go and whether Dwayne's band needed a riser. In the corner sat the one thing left from her house on Hope Road, which we had finished emptying that morning: a battered upright piano. My mother lifted its lid and played the first bars of the hymn she had used to end every school assembly, and I, Roshane, remembered sitting cross-legged on this very floor, listening to her. When she closed the lid, we did not return to the tables at once. Instead we measured again, this time to find a space beside the stage where the piano could stand on the day itself. Outside, a groundskeeper was chalking white lines across the football pitch.
g.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It moves from routine planning to a memory sparked by an object, then back to reshaped planning.

It presents the daughter's doubts about the wedding and then shows her mother easing them.
